# Introduction

Low-surface-brightness galaxies are under-represented in every major galaxy
catalogue, and the deficit traces the selection functions of the surveys the
catalogues are built from [@zaritsky2019]. Recent work has treated their
identification as a deep-learning problem: @tanoglidis2021 trained
convolutional networks ("DeepShadows") to separate LSB galaxies from imaging
artifacts in the Dark Energy Survey, establishing a benchmark on
visually-labelled data.

Convolutional architectures are motivated by the absence of a known good
feature basis. For galaxies, however, a strong prior exists: their light is
approximately elliptically symmetric, and departures from that symmetry are
themselves informative. A representation that bins light in concentric annuli
encodes the symmetry directly instead of asking a network to learn it from
data. This paper tests whether that representation, with an off-the-shelf
classifier, matches the pixel-based deep model. We then construct a
survey-scale catalogue with an explicit cut-based selection; the classifier is
used operationally only to order candidates for per-object verification, and
because every candidate is verified, no classifier score enters the catalogue
definition.

The result of the application is DEBBIE (Dual Ensemble of Boosted trees and
Bidirectional recurrent networks for Identifying Extragalactic sources), a catalogue of {{N_COMMA}}
galaxy candidates in DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR10 [@dey2019] with no prior
identification as galaxies in the catalogues and services queried. The
selection function is measured on real catalogued galaxies instead of
synthetic injections (Section 5.5), and the full selection can be recomputed
from a released 3.2 GB source extract.

# Data

## Survey data

We use the DR10 south *sweep* catalogues: the survey's own Tractor
photometry [@lang2016],
comprising positions, morphological types, shape parameters, and forced
photometry in $g$, $r$, $z$, and the WISE bands. We deliberately select from
the survey's measurements instead of re-detecting sources in the imaging;
Section 5.5 measures what that choice gives up in completeness.

The main catalogue footprint is DR10 south at galactic latitude
$|b| \ge 30^\circ$: all 874 sweep files in that region were processed, an
occupied area of approximately {{AREA_COMMA}} deg$^2$. That latitude bound is
physical: at lower latitude, galactic cirrus reproduces the morphology of
diffuse galaxies and foreground extinction corrupts the surface-brightness
selection. These cuts and the screening of the next subsection define the
catalogue on their own; the Section 4 classifier prioritised the verification
order and does not affect membership. Sweeps at
$12^\circ < |b| < 30^\circ$ were also processed; the
{{N_EXT_COMMA}} candidates they yield are released as a separately flagged
extension, inherit a cirrus-contamination caveat, and enter none of the
statistics reported here.

## Benchmark data

Classifier comparisons use the DeepShadows sample [@tanoglidis2021],
restricted to their objects and to their visually-confirmed hard negative
class (`artifact_hard_visually_rejected`), which is the class their published
AUC is evaluated against. Including the easier SVM-rejected negatives inflates
the AUC of every method by approximately 0.014 and is avoided.

The comparison is asymmetric in two ways. One favours the published model:
it was trained on 30,000 objects, against 10,121 available to ours. The other
is unavoidable: the CNN operates on DES imagery with DES photometry, while we
measure the same sky positions in DR10 imaging with our own measurement chain.
The comparison is therefore between complete pipelines on shared labels, not
between two classifiers on shared features; the controlled representation
comparison in Section 4.2 is internal to our pipeline.

# The radial representation

Each source is measured in 24 concentric annuli with geometrically spaced
radii, each divided into 32 position-angle cells, in each of $g$, $r$, and
$z$. Per annulus we retain the mean and the median over position angle, and the
amplitudes of the first four azimuthal Fourier modes, by discrete Fourier
transform over those cells [following the
long-standing use of low-order Fourier terms in isophote analysis;
@jedrzejewski1987; @rix1995], which encode lopsidedness
and ellipticity without a shape fit. We keep the median as well as the mean
because it is robust to a single bright neighbour occupying one wedge. Cell
coverage is tracked against the count each cell would have if the frame were
complete, so that brick-edge clipping registers as reduced coverage and not as
a spuriously faint annulus. Profiles are extracted twice, at the
catalogue position and at a flux-weighted refined centroid; both are retained,
and the offset between the two centres is a feature (a large offset
flags blends and fragments; [Fig. @fig-representation]). Classifiers use library-default hyperparameters
with no per-benchmark tuning; splits, seeds, and feature definitions are in
the released code.

![The representation, illustrated on a catalogue object using the released
colour image (the production pipeline operates on calibrated FITS pixels):
cutout (left), the annulus-by-position-angle grid (centre), and the resulting
radial profile (right).](figures/fig1_representation.png){#fig-representation}

# Classification results

## Benchmark

On a balanced test set of 3,340 objects (1,670 per class), split by object and
evaluated once, gradient-boosted trees on the radial representation reach AUC
0.9810 with a 2,000-resample bootstrap interval of [0.9765, 0.9852]. The
published CNN reports 0.9740 [0.9700, 0.9740] on the same object and negative
classes. The identical classifier on the six conventional catalogue features used in
our production screening (profile monotonicity, concentration, signal-to-noise
ratio, angular radius, central surface brightness, and local imaging depth)
reaches 0.9098 [0.9002, 0.9198] ([Fig. @fig-benchmark]). Classifiers are
XGBoost 3.4.0 and scikit-learn 1.9.0 with library defaults; splits and seeds
are fixed in the released code.

![AUC on the DeepShadows benchmark. The gain over conventional features comes
from the representation; the classifier is identical in both of our
rows.](figures/fig2_benchmark.png){#fig-benchmark}

## Representation versus architecture

The representation is separated from the model by a controlled ablation:
the same gradient-boosted classifier, the same folds, four feature sets, and
nothing varying but what the classifier is shown. One fold is held out by sky
position rather than at random, so that no field contributes to both sides of
the split; we call it the frozen spatial fold and use it wherever a single
number is quoted. On that fold, six conventional catalogue features score
0.9022, the per-annulus profile alone (144 features) 0.9645, that profile plus
the six catalogue features (150) 0.9674, and the full flattened representation
(1,023) 0.9775.

A single fold cannot carry this claim, because the fold-to-fold spread of a
fixed model on this data is about 0.05, comparable to the effect being
measured. We therefore repeated all four arms over five stratified folds, with
every arm scored on every fold (@tbl-ablation). The ordering is identical on
all five, and the paired gain from six catalogue features to the full
representation is $+0.062 \pm 0.003$, never falling below $+0.059$ on any
fold. The pairing is what matters: fold difficulty is common to all four
arms and cancels in the difference, so the relevant uncertainty is the 0.003
spread of the paired gain and not the 0.05 spread of absolute AUCs.

| feature set | features | mean AUC | sd |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| six catalogue features | 6 | 0.9244 | 0.0028 |
| per-annulus profile | 144 | 0.9801 | 0.0020 |
| profile + six catalogue features | 150 | 0.9819 | 0.0019 |
| full flattened representation | 1,023 | 0.9869 | 0.0009 |

: Four-arm ablation over five stratified folds, identical classifier and
folds throughout. {#tbl-ablation}

Two caveats bound the ablation. These folds are randomly stratified, not
spatially held out, so the absolute values are optimistic relative to the
frozen spatial fold above, as the two sets of numbers show, and only the
paired comparison is claimed. And the ablation establishes that the
representation carries information the six catalogue features do not; it does
not establish that any particular architecture exploits it best. We make no
architecture claim. A recurrent model was also trained on this data and scores
0.9780 on the frozen spatial fold, against 0.9775 for the trees, but the frozen
artefact does not record which feature set it consumed, so that number cannot be
paired with any row here.

# The DEBBIE catalogue

## Selection

From the sweep catalogues we select sources with a resolved morphological type
(`EXP`, `DEV`, `SER`, `REX`; Tractor assigns `SHAPE_R` = 0 to PSF sources, so
this excludes point sources exactly), $r_{\rm eff} \ge 3''$, mean surface
brightness within the effective radius $\mu_{\rm eff}$ between 24.0 and 26.5
mag arcsec$^{-2}$ in $g$, at least two exposures in both $g$ and $r$, a $z$-band detection (a weaker,
single-epoch requirement, retained because $z$-band epoch counts are lower
over parts of the southern footprint), and `MASKBITS` = 0. The faint boundary of the
surface-brightness window matters most: above $\mu_{\rm eff} = 26.5$, Tractor
increasingly fits large radii to noise fluctuations, and in 48-object contact-sheet inspections of an early pool, sources above
this threshold predominantly rendered as background fluctuations (62% of that
pool lay above it).

## Novelty screening

Candidates are screened positionally, at 20$''$, against 110,190,191
catalogued objects held locally: the full HyperLEDA catalogue [@makarov2014],
SDSS DR12 galaxies over the footprint [@alam2015], GLADE+ [@dalya2022], the
2MASS Extended Source Catalog [@jarrett2000], and SMUDGes [@zaritsky2019]. Local screening runs at $4.5\times10^{5}$ positions s$^{-1}$, which
permits screening every candidate. Survivors
are then queried individually against NED, SIMBAD, and SMUDGes. An object
whose query fails is marked unverified and re-queried; a failed check is never
recorded as novelty.

Two further filters address failure modes identified during inspection.
Tractor shreds extended sources, so an outer
fragment can sit more than 20$''$ from the catalogued position. We remove
fragments of large galaxies by rejecting any candidate with an entry of
the 110-million-object index between 20$''$ and 45$''$. That filter also
discards genuine candidates by chance coincidence: at 20,000 random footprint
positions, 22.2%
have an index entry in that annulus, so roughly one in five genuine candidates
is removed by an unrelated neighbour. The selection function of Section 5.5
does *not* capture that loss, because it measures the photometric cuts alone.
The second filter removes spurious detections clustered on defective imaging
bricks, rejecting any candidate with three or more other candidates within
1.5$'$. One region of 6$'$ radius at $(\alpha, \delta) = (144.79^\circ,
-2.79^\circ)$ is excluded permanently, after visual confirmation that the
brick is defective.

Duplicate entries arising when Tractor
splits one galaxy into several rows are merged with a matching radius of
$\max(6'', r_{\rm eff})$, retaining the largest member; 2,013 entries were
merged. Objects whose NED or SIMBAD queries could not be completed after
retries are excluded from the catalogue entirely, so a query failure can
suppress a real candidate but cannot create a spurious one.

## The nature of the claim

The objects in DEBBIE carry no prior extragalactic identification of any
type, under an operational definition: an object counts as identified if it
appears in
HyperLEDA (non-stellar), the SDSS DR12 galaxy class, GLADE+, the 2MASS XSC, or
SMUDGes, or is typed as any extragalactic object (G, GPair, GTrpl, GGroup, QSO, AGN)
by NED or SIMBAD [@wenger2000]; prior designations are collected from NED
within 0.5$'$ of each position and recorded per object.

One screen is absent without changing the count, and must still be
disclosed: VST ATLAS DR4 [@shanks2025] classifies 98.55% of the entries it
detects here as galaxies, and it was not queried. As with VII/292 below, that
is a bulk automated morphological classification applied to every source in a
survey footprint, not an identification of an individual object, so we
do not treat it as prior identification and remove nothing for it. A reader
who takes the opposite view should add it to the reasons to read this
catalogue as classification rather than discovery.

A second screen was missing entirely, and it does change the count. DESI DR1
[@desidr1], a public spectroscopic release covering this same imaging
footprint and selecting its targets from this same parent photometry, was not
among the catalogues queried. Matching the catalogue against it at 2$''$
finds a reliable spectrum (ZWARN = 0) for {{DESI_MAIN}} main-catalogue
entries, {{DESI_MAIN_PCT}}% of the set, of which
{{DESI_GAL}} are typed GALAXY and {{DESI_QSO}} QSO. Those objects carry a
published spectroscopic extragalactic identification and are therefore not
previously unidentified under our own definition. They are removed in v1.2,
leaving {{N12}} entries, and every number in this paper is computed on the
remaining set. The released tables mark every affected row.

It is tempting to read the same match as a purity measurement, and we
explicitly do not. Of the {{DESI_REL}} main-set entries with a reliable DESI
classification, {{DESI_PURITY}}% are extragalactic and {{DESI_STAR}} are
stars. That figure cannot be extrapolated to the catalogue. Every matched row
is a deliberate DESI target, and DESI selects its targets from this same
Legacy photometry using cuts (BGS, LRG, ELG) that are themselves galaxy
selections. The measured quantity is therefore "of our candidates that DESI's
galaxy selection also chose, what fraction are galaxies", which is largely
determined by the purity of DESI's selection rather than of ours: the
selection into the measured subsample is conditioned on the property being
measured. The number is a fact about those {{DESI_REL}} objects, each of which
has a spectrum, and those objects are precisely the ones removed from the
catalogue for not being novel. It says nothing about the {{N_REMAIN}}
entries that remain. Catalogue purity is unmeasured.

A further consequence of the novelty definition cuts against the claim.
cuts against the claim. {{VII292_PRESENT}}% of the catalogue appears in VII/292 [@duncan2022],
the published DESI Legacy photometric-redshift catalogue from which we draw
{{N_LSP_COMMA}} of our own redshifts, and of the entries there carrying a
star/galaxy probability, {{VII292_NONSTELLAR}}% are assigned $p_{\rm star} < 0.5$. In that
narrow sense a published catalogue has already treated most of these sources
as non-stellar, and we rely on it while claiming novelty. Our position is
that a bulk value-added catalogue, which assigns a photometric redshift and a
star/galaxy probability to every source in the parent imaging including
stars and artefacts, does not constitute identification of an individual
object as a galaxy: no such entry is a claim about a particular object, none
is ingested by NED or SIMBAD as an extragalactic classification, and none
would support a designation. Readers who take the opposite view should read
this catalogue as the classification of already-detected sources instead of
the discovery of new ones. We regard that reading as legitimate, and it is
why the title claims absence of prior identification rather than novelty of
detection. NED aggregates the identifications of most
published extragalactic surveys, which is the substantive basis of the claim;
we do not claim exhaustiveness over catalogues outside these services. Nearly
all entries ({{DESIG_PCT}}%) coincide with an automated detection in at least one all-sky
survey, most commonly WISE [@wright2010], and these prior designations are recorded
per object. The claim is that no queried publication or catalogue has classified the
object as a galaxy. @zaritsky2019 assigned SMDG designations to roughly 7,000
objects from this same imaging on the same basis.

## Physical properties

Redshifts are available for {{Z_COV}}% of the catalogue, and after the DESI
removal none of them are spectroscopic: the {{N_SPEC_PREV_COMMA}} spectroscopic redshifts the
catalogue previously carried were DESI's own, and left with the objects they
belonged to. This is a photometric-redshift catalogue, and every distance-
dependent quantity below inherits that. {{N_LSP_COMMA}} come from the Legacy
Surveys photometric redshift catalogue [@zou2019] matched through the CDS X-Match service [@boch2012], and
{{N_OWN_COMMA}} from a gradient-boosted photometric redshift trained on our
own $g r z W1$ photometry for sky the public photo-$z$ does not cover
($\sigma_{\rm NMAD} = 0.046$ against the Legacy photo-$z$ on spatially
held-out sky; a shuffled-label control degrades to 0.194). The photo-$z$
source is recorded per object, and the two photometric estimates are never
merged in any analysis that depends on redshift
quality.

Distances assume flat $\Lambda$CDM with $H_0 = 70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$
and $\Omega_m = 0.3$; absolute magnitudes are not k-corrected; stellar masses
use the $g{-}r$ colour mass-to-light relation of @bell2003 and are
factor-of-two estimates. The median catalogue object lies at
$z = {{Z_MED3}}$ with
$r_{\rm eff} = {{R_KPC}}$ kpc, $M_g = {{MG_MED}}$, and
$\log(M_\star/M_\odot) = {{LOGM_MED}}$. These are the parameters of ordinary
galaxies, not dwarfs, and the explanation is cosmological surface-brightness
dimming: the bolometric Tolman factor is
$2.5\log_{10}(1+z)^{4} = 10\log_{10}(1+z) = {{TOLMAN}}$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$ at
the median redshift, and for a band-limited specific intensity the
corresponding factor, $7.5\log_{10}(1+z)$, is {{TOLMAN3}} mag arcsec$^{-2}$.
Either value is a substantial fraction of the 2.5-mag selection window, so an
intrinsically normal galaxy at the median redshift enters the window without
being intrinsically diffuse. K-corrections are not applied; the argument
concerns the population, not any individual object. The
catalogue should be read as a census of previously uncatalogued galaxy
candidates, most of them distant and dimmed, not of intrinsically
diffuse systems. The exception is the nearby tail: {{N_DWARF_COMMA}} objects
at $z < 0.05$, with median $r_{\rm eff} = {{DWARF_RKPC}}$ kpc and median
$\log(M_\star/M_\odot) = {{DWARF_LOGM}}$, dwarf sizes and masses. Of these, {{N_UDG_COMMA}} satisfy $r_{\rm eff} > 1.5$ kpc and
mean $\mu_{\rm eff} > 24$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, approximating the
ultra-diffuse criteria of @vandokkum2015, which are conventionally stated in
central rather than mean surface brightness.

## Selection function

The selection function is measured against real catalogued galaxies rather
than synthetic injections: for each known galaxy inside the observed
footprint, we ask whether the sweeps contain a resolved counterpart and
whether the *photometric cuts* retain it. Real profiles, neighbours, and
imaging defects enter at their true rates. The measurement covers the cuts
only; the novelty screen, the fragment and clump filters, and the
verification-completeness term of [@sec-verifcomp] are all excluded from it.

The reference population is the non-stellar entries of the same
110-million-object screening index, restricted to $|b| \ge 30^\circ$ and to
sky the extract covers, matched at 3$''$. Of 235,715 such galaxies, 33,595
appear in the source extract as resolved sources with
$r_{\rm eff} \ge 2''$; of those, in 15 of the 17
populated cells inside the selection window the photometric cuts alone retain between 70% and
89% of them ([Fig. @fig-sky]b); the remaining two cells are 56%
(8--10$''$, $\mu$ 24--25) and 63% (10--15$''$, $\mu$ 24--25). Cell-wise Wilson 95% intervals are 0.1--9
percentage points (half-width) for cells with at least 50 galaxies and are
included in `selection_function.json` in the release. Above $r_{\rm eff} = 15''$ only one of 34 known galaxies survives. With
$N = 34$ the Wilson 95% interval is 0.5--14.9%, wider than the point estimate,
so this bounds the retention without measuring it. The cause is not in doubt:
Tractor shreds the largest galaxies and the fragment filter then removes the
pieces. DEBBIE is
therefore substantially incomplete above $r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$ and
cannot constrain the abundance of large LSB systems.

### Verification completeness {#sec-verifcomp}

The selection function above is not the end-to-end one, and the difference is
large enough to state separately. Candidates enter the catalogue only after a
per-object novelty check, and that check did not run on the whole candidate
pool. Of {{POOL_HI}} candidates passing the cuts at $|b| \ge 30^\circ$,
{{POOL_VER}} were checked and {{POOL_UNVER}} ({{POOL_UNVER_PCT}}%) were not,
because per-object queries are excluded once their retries are exhausted.

That loss is not uniform in size. The checked fraction falls monotonically
from 74.8% at $r_{\rm eff} = 3$--4$''$ to 73.5% (4--6$''$), 59.6%
(6--10$''$) and 49.4% (10--15$''$): the largest candidates are the least
likely to have been checked, plausibly because they have more catalogued
neighbours and so generate the slowest and most failure-prone queries.
End-to-end, the selection fraction is therefore approximately the product of the
cut retention and this term: near 10--15$''$ roughly $0.63 \times 0.49
\approx 0.31$, not 0.63. Correspondingly, the incompleteness above
$r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$ reported earlier is a joint
statement about the fragment filter and this bias, not about the sky.
{{UNVER_BIG}} unchecked candidates with $r_{\rm eff} \ge 6''$ remain in the
pool; they are released with the extract so that the omission is auditable.

Two limits bound the selection function of Section 5.5. It is
completeness relative to *known* galaxies; a population absent from both
published catalogues and the sweeps is invisible to it. And it cannot be
decomposed into detection and selection terms, because the archived source
extract retains only sources with $r_{\rm eff} \ge 2''$. The raw sweeps that
would allow the decomposition are no longer held.

The catalogue is also not spatially uniform: source density falls by a factor of two to four in the band
$-2^\circ < \delta < +2^\circ$ ({{DEC_B1}} and {{DEC_B2}} objects in the
two equatorial 2$^\circ$ bins, against {{DEC_NBR_LO}}--{{DEC_NBR_HI}} in the
six neighbouring bins), where prior cataloguing in the screening pool is
densest (the SDSS equatorial stripes, including Stripe 82), so a
larger fraction of candidates there is screened out as already catalogued.
Clustering analyses must model this.

![Left: the {{N_COMMA}} catalogue objects on the sky. Right: the selection
fraction for known galaxies present in the sweeps, as a function of size and
surface brightness; bins with fewer than 50 galaxies are
starred.](figures/fig3_sky_selection.png){#fig-sky}

## Purity

Purity has not been measured by visual inspection. What the catalogue looks
like can still be shown, and [Fig. @fig-montage] shows it from both ends: eight
selected entries above, eight drawn at random below. A {{PURITY_N_COMMA}}-object sample stratified over
{{PURITY_CELLS}} cells of the ($r_{\rm eff}$, $\mu_{\rm eff}$) plane is
reserved for that, weighted so the unbiased catalogue total can be
reconstructed, with an effective size of {{PURITY_NEFF_COMMA}}. One
independent instrument does constrain purity in the meantime. VST ATLAS DR4
[@shanks2025] images part of this footprint with a different telescope,
pipeline and seeing, and, unlike a spectroscopic target list, catalogues
everything it detects, stars and noise included, so selection into the matched
sample is on detectability rather than on the property being measured.
Matching 20,000 random catalogue positions at 2$''$ returns a counterpart for
28.0%, and of those 98.55% carry `MERGEDCLASS` galaxy or probable galaxy,
1.04% star or probable star, and 0.41% noise: an implied contamination of
1.45% (95% CI 1.14--1.76%).

Three limits stop this being the purity measurement. The matched subset is
0.21 mag brighter than the unmatched remainder, so it under-samples the faint
end where contamination should concentrate. VST's classifier and ours both
rest on morphological star--galaxy separation, so they are correlated methods,
not independent tests. And the match reaches only the 28% of the
catalogue inside the VST ATLAS footprint.

A second external check bounds contamination from below. Gaia DR3, which enters
the pipeline nowhere, has a counterpart at 1.84% of 20,000 random catalogue
positions, and 0.79% (95% CI 0.67--0.91%) show 5$\sigma$ parallax or proper
motion and are therefore certainly stars. That is a hard lower bound and a weak
one: implied total magnitudes are median $g = 20.8$ and only 18.1% of the
catalogue is brighter than $g = 20$, where Gaia astrometry is reliable. Within
that Gaia-sensitive subset the star rate is about 4.4%. Extrapolating it, rather
than the 0.79%, is the relevant comparison, and it leaves plausible
contamination at several percent, which does not contradict the
$p_{\rm star}$ expectation of {{PSTAR_EXP_PCT}}%.

As a further interim expectation, treating the Legacy Surveys $p_{\rm star}$
as a calibrated probability gives $\sum_i p_{{\rm star},i} =$
{{PSTAR_EXP_COMMA}} expected stellar contaminants ({{PSTAR_EXP_PCT}}%);
{{PSTAR_COMMA}} entries ({{PSTAR_PCT}}%) individually exceed
$p_{\rm star} = 0.5$ and carry a flag. Entries are retained with the flag,
not removed.

# Data availability

The catalogue is released as `DEBBIE.csv` ({{N_COMMA}} rows) with
`DEBBIE_lowb_extension.csv` ({{N_EXT_COMMA}} rows), version 1.2, each with an
accompanying ECSV and SHA-256 checksum, containing designations, positions,
sizes, surface brightnesses, colours, Sérsic indices, redshifts with per-object
provenance, physical sizes, absolute magnitudes, stellar-mass estimates, and
all prior automated designations. Designation numbers are stable across
versions by construction and the sequence is not contiguous (merged duplicates
retire their numbers). The full selection can be recomputed from the released
3.2 GB distilled source table (33.5 million resolved sources, 31 columns),
which reproduces the catalogue exactly.

# Limitations

Photometry is Tractor's [@lang2016] and is not independently remeasured.
{{OWN_PCT}}% of redshifts derive from our own photometric estimator, which is
trained on photometric labels; its quoted scatter is measured against the
Legacy photo-$z$, not against spectroscopy, and these values are suitable for
population statistics only. None of the redshifts are spectroscopic.
Purity is unmeasured: the stratified visual sample reserved for it has not yet
been inspected. The
selection inherits Tractor's own detection incompleteness, collapses above
$r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$, excludes $|b| < 30^\circ$ entirely, and is
spatially non-uniform where prior surveys are deepest.
